<properties>
{"title":"74. BRST symmetry"}
</properties>
<content>
In this section we will rederive the gauge-fixed path integral for nonabelian gauge theory from a different point of view. We will discover that the complete gauge-fixed lagrangian, $`\mathcal { L } \equiv \mathcal { L } _ { \mathrm { { Y M } } } + \mathcal { L } _ { \mathrm { { g f } } } + \mathcal { L } _ { \mathrm { { g h } } }`$ , still has a residual form of the gauge symmetry, known as Becchi–Rouet–Stora–Tyutin symmetry, or BRST symmetry for short. BRST symmetry can be used to derive the Slavnov–Taylor identities that, among other useful things, show that the coupling constant is renormalized by the same factor at each of its appearances in $`\mathcal { L }`$ . Also, we can use BRST symmetry to show that gluons whose polarizations are not both spacelike and transverse (perpendicular to the four-momentum) decouple from physical scattering amplitudes (as do particles that are created by the ghost field).
Consider a nonabelian gauge theory with a gauge field $`A _ { \mu } ^ { a } ( x )`$ , and a scalar or spinor field $`\phi _ { i } ( x )`$ in the representation R. Then, under an infinitesimal gauge transformation parameterized by $`\theta ^ { a } ( x )`$ , we have
<synced_block url="https://app.notion.com/p/51a0dad3c8454b07a2087d974003aaf0#4a2effeb04d54086b2fb09a7d7a61162">
	$$
	\begin{array} { l } { { \delta A _ { \mu } ^ { a } ( x ) = - D ^ { a b } \theta ^ { b } ( x ) \ , } } \\{ { { } } } \\{ { \delta \phi _ { i } ( x ) = - i g \theta ^ { a } ( x ) ( T _ { \mathrm { { R } } } ^ { a } ) _ { i j } \phi _ { j } ( x ) \ . } } \end{array} \tag{74.1-74.2}
	$$
</synced_block>
We now introduce a scalar Grassmann field $`c ^ { a } ( x )`$ in the adjoint representation; this field will turn out to be the ghost field that we introduced in section 71. We define an infinitesimal BRST transformation via
<synced_block url="https://app.notion.com/p/51a0dad3c8454b07a2087d974003aaf0#0bef5aa39da842198bc310d8d180dcac">
	$$
	\begin{array} { l } { { \delta _ { \mathrm { { s } } } A _ { \mu } ^ { a } ( x ) \equiv D _ { \mu } ^ { a b } c ^ { b } ( x ) } } \\{ { { } } } \\{ { { } = \partial _ { \mu } c ^ { a } ( x ) - g f ^ { a b c } A _ { \mu } ^ { c } ( x ) c ^ { b } ( x ) , } } \end{array} \tag{74.3}
	$$
</synced_block>
<synced_block url="https://app.notion.com/p/51a0dad3c8454b07a2087d974003aaf0#ed9d23b21a044ed78b6d0eb9ad9aa45a">
	$$
	\delta _ { \mathrm B } \phi _ { i } ( x ) \equiv i g c ^ { a } ( x ) ( T _ { \mathrm { R } } ^ { a } ) _ { i j } \phi _ { j } ( x ) . \tag{74.4-74.5}
	$$
</synced_block>
This is simply an infinitesimal gauge transformation, with the ghost field $`c ^ { a } ( x )`$ in place of the infinitesimal parameter $`- \theta ^ { a } ( x )`$ . Therefore, any combination of fields that is gauge invariant is also BRST invariant. In particular, the Yang–Mills lagrangian $`\mathcal { L } _ { \mathrm { v M } }`$ (including the appropriate lagrangian for the scalar or spinor field $`\phi _ { i }`$ ) is BRST invariant,
<synced_block url="https://app.notion.com/p/51a0dad3c8454b07a2087d974003aaf0#dcd6cbb126bd4b31a730d87c1484f9bb">
	$$
	\delta _ { \scriptscriptstyle \mathrm { B } } \mathcal { L } _ { \mathrm { Y M } } = 0 . \tag{74.6}
	$$
</synced_block>
We now place a further restriction on the BRST transformation: we require a BRST variation of a BRST variation to be zero. This requirement will determine the BRST transformation of the ghost field. Consider
<synced_block url="https://app.notion.com/p/51a0dad3c8454b07a2087d974003aaf0#f4e34affa93f4340940685bfecc29378">
	$$
	\delta _ { \mathrm { { B } } } ( \delta _ { \mathrm { { B } } } \phi _ { i } ) = i g ( \delta _ { \mathrm { { B } } } c ^ { a } ) ( T _ { \mathrm { { R } } } ^ { a } ) _ { i j } \phi _ { j } - i g c ^ { a } ( T _ { \mathrm { { R } } } ^ { a } ) _ { i j } \delta _ { \mathrm { { B } } } \phi _ { j } ~ . \tag{74.7}
	$$
</synced_block>
There is a minus sign in front of the second term because $`\delta _ { \mathrm { B } }`$ acts as an anticommuting object, and it generates a minus sign when it passes through another anticommuting object, in this case $`c ^ { a }`$ . Using eq. (74.5), we have
<callout color="gray_bg">
	<synced_block url="https://app.notion.com/p/51a0dad3c8454b07a2087d974003aaf0#8552c571ea6b4dd486a9391306d7688d">
		$$
		\delta _ { \mathrm B } \phi _ { i } ( x ) \equiv i g c ^ { a } ( x ) ( T _ { \mathrm { R } } ^ { a } ) _ { i j } \phi _ { j } ( x ) . \tag{74.4-74.5}
		$$
	</synced_block>
</callout>
<synced_block url="https://app.notion.com/p/51a0dad3c8454b07a2087d974003aaf0#dd8934ac93344a2ca4f930e945aed7fe">
	$$
	\begin{array} { r } { \delta _ { \mathtt { B } } \big ( \delta _ { \mathtt { B } } \phi _ { i } \big ) = i g ( \delta _ { \mathtt { B } } c ^ { a } ) ( T _ { \mathtt { R } } ^ { a } ) _ { i j } \phi _ { j } - g ^ { 2 } c ^ { a } c ^ { b } ( T _ { \mathtt { R } } ^ { a } T _ { \mathtt { R } } ^ { b } ) _ { i k } \phi _ { k } . } \end{array} \tag{74.8}
	$$
</synced_block>
We now use $`c ^ { b } c ^ { a } = - c ^ { a } c ^ { b }`$ in the second term to replace $`T _ { \mathrm { R } } ^ { a } T _ { \mathrm { R } } ^ { b }`$ with its antisymmetric part, $`\textstyle { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } [ T _ { \mathrm { { R } } } ^ { a } , T _ { \mathrm { { R } } } ^ { b } ] = { \frac { i } { 2 } } f ^ { a b c } T _ { \mathrm { { R } } } ^ { c }`$ . Then, after relabeling some dummy indices, we have
<synced_block url="https://app.notion.com/p/51a0dad3c8454b07a2087d974003aaf0#6672a0dcb0f24dc2a87dbecfe0a3fc1c">
	$$
	\begin{array} { r } { \delta _ { \mathtt { B } } ( \delta _ { \mathtt { B } } \phi _ { i } ) = i g ( \delta _ { \mathtt { B } } c ^ { c } + \frac { 1 } { 2 } g f ^ { a b c } c ^ { a } c ^ { b } ) ( T _ { \mathtt { R } } ^ { c } ) _ { i j } \phi _ { j } . } \end{array} \tag{74.9}
	$$
</synced_block>
The right-hand side of eq. (74.9) will vanish for all $`\phi _ { j } ( x )`$ if and only if
<callout color="gray_bg">
	<synced_block url="https://app.notion.com/p/51a0dad3c8454b07a2087d974003aaf0#7d3f4094b69b4361b57f78251a1544a4">
		$$
		\begin{array} { r } { \delta _ { \mathtt { B } } ( \delta _ { \mathtt { B } } \phi _ { i } ) = i g ( \delta _ { \mathtt { B } } c ^ { c } + \frac { 1 } { 2 } g f ^ { a b c } c ^ { a } c ^ { b } ) ( T _ { \mathtt { R } } ^ { c } ) _ { i j } \phi _ { j } . } \end{array} \tag{74.9}
		$$
	</synced_block>
</callout>
<synced_block url="https://app.notion.com/p/51a0dad3c8454b07a2087d974003aaf0#11fdf0bf1e11498891cdb5924d684e3f">
	$$
	\delta _ { \mathrm { B } } c ^ { c } ( x ) = - { \textstyle \frac { 1 } { 2 } } g f ^ { a b c } c ^ { a } ( x ) c ^ { b } ( x ) . \tag{74.10}
	$$
</synced_block>
We therefore adopt eq. (74.10) as the BRST variation of the ghost field.
<callout color="gray_bg">
	<synced_block url="https://app.notion.com/p/51a0dad3c8454b07a2087d974003aaf0#1bab07f525074e5ea3c678acda5c29f9">
		$$
		\delta _ { \mathrm { B } } c ^ { c } ( x ) = - { \textstyle \frac { 1 } { 2 } } g f ^ { a b c } c ^ { a } ( x ) c ^ { b } ( x ) . \tag{74.10}
		$$
	</synced_block>
</callout>
Let us now check to see that the BRST variation of the BRST variation of the gauge field also vanishes. From eq. (74.4) we have
<callout color="gray_bg">
	<synced_block url="https://app.notion.com/p/51a0dad3c8454b07a2087d974003aaf0#801b68a48596452ebc311fb238376f08">
		$$
		\delta _ { \mathrm B } \phi _ { i } ( x ) \equiv i g c ^ { a } ( x ) ( T _ { \mathrm { R } } ^ { a } ) _ { i j } \phi _ { j } ( x ) . \tag{74.4-74.5}
		$$
	</synced_block>
</callout>
<synced_block url="https://app.notion.com/p/51a0dad3c8454b07a2087d974003aaf0#e1380a564f014893abf96c12388ca9ff">
	$$
	\begin{array} { l } { { \delta _ { \scriptscriptstyle \mathrm { B } } ( \delta _ { \scriptscriptstyle \mathrm { B } } A _ { \mu } ^ { a } ) = ( \delta ^ { a b } \partial _ { \mu } - g f ^ { a b c } A _ { \mu } ^ { c } ) ( \delta _ { \scriptscriptstyle \mathrm { B } } c ^ { b } ) - g f ^ { a b c } ( \delta _ { \scriptscriptstyle \mathrm { B } } A _ { \mu } ^ { c } ) c ^ { b } } } \\{ { { } } } \\{ { { } = D _ { \mu } ^ { a b } ( \delta _ { \scriptscriptstyle \mathrm { B } } c ^ { b } ) - g f ^ { a b c } ( D _ { \mu } ^ { c d } c ^ { d } ) c ^ { b } } } \\{ { { } } } \\{ { { } = D _ { \mu } ^ { a b } ( \delta _ { \scriptscriptstyle \mathrm { B } } c ^ { b } ) - g f ^ { a b c } ( \partial _ { \mu } c ^ { c } ) c ^ { b } + g ^ { 2 } f ^ { a b c } f ^ { c d e } A _ { \mu } ^ { e } c ^ { d } c ^ { b } . } } \end{array} \tag{74.11}
	$$
</synced_block>
We now use the antisymmetry of $`f ^ { a b c }`$ in the second term to replace $`( \partial _ { \mu } c ^ { c } ) c ^ { b }`$ with its antisymmetric part,
<synced_block url="https://app.notion.com/p/51a0dad3c8454b07a2087d974003aaf0#e1cbd32eb3f14bf0b3bb6399c85ed649">
	$$
	\begin{array} { c } { { ( \partial _ { \mu } c ^ { [ c } ) c ^ { b ] } \equiv \frac { 1 } { 2 } ( \partial _ { \mu } c ^ { c } ) c ^ { b } - \frac { 1 } { 2 } ( \partial _ { \mu } c ^ { b } ) c ^ { c } } } \\{ { { } } } \\{ { = \frac { 1 } { 2 } ( \partial _ { \mu } c ^ { c } ) c ^ { b } + \frac { 1 } { 2 } c ^ { c } ( \partial _ { \mu } c ^ { b } ) } } \\{ { { } } } \\{ { { } = \frac { 1 } { 2 } \partial _ { \mu } ( c ^ { c } c ^ { b } ) . } } \end{array} \tag{74.12}
	$$
</synced_block>
Similarly, we use the antisymmetry of $`c ^ { d } c ^ { b }`$ in the third term to replace $`f ^ { a b c } f ^ { c d e }`$ with its antisymmetric part,
<synced_block url="https://app.notion.com/p/51a0dad3c8454b07a2087d974003aaf0#00ef90ffbcec4eb4847b6c0a9bcfa1d4">
	$$
	\begin{array} { r l } & { \frac { 1 } { 2 } ( f ^ { a b c } f ^ { c d e } - f ^ { a d c } f ^ { c b e } ) = - \frac { 1 } { 2 } [ ( T _ { \mathrm { \scriptscriptstyle A } } ^ { b } ) ^ { a c } ( T _ { \mathrm { \scriptscriptstyle A } } ^ { d } ) ^ { c e } - ( T _ { \mathrm { \scriptscriptstyle A } } ^ { d } ) ^ { a c } ( T _ { \mathrm { \scriptscriptstyle A } } ^ { b } ) ^ { c e } ] } \\& { \phantom { \frac { 1 } { 2 } ( } = - \frac { 1 } { 2 } i f ^ { b d h } ( T _ { \mathrm { \scriptscriptstyle A } } ^ { h } ) ^ { a e } } \\& { \phantom { \frac { 1 } { 2 } ( } = - \frac { 1 } { 2 } f ^ { b d h } f ^ { h a e } , } \end{array} \tag{74.13}
	$$
</synced_block>
which is just the Jacobi identity. Now we have
<synced_block url="https://app.notion.com/p/51a0dad3c8454b07a2087d974003aaf0#a1b98f7f7f7b4c90895fa6bd21bebdfc">
	$$
	\begin{array} { l } { { \delta _ { \scriptscriptstyle \mathrm { B } } ( \delta _ { \scriptscriptstyle \mathrm { B } } A _ { \mu } ^ { a } ) = D _ { \mu } ^ { a b } ( \delta _ { \scriptscriptstyle \mathrm { B } } c ^ { b } ) - { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } g f ^ { a b c } ( \partial _ { \mu } c ^ { c } c ^ { b } ) - { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } g ^ { 2 } f ^ { b d h } f ^ { h a e } A _ { \mu } ^ { e } c ^ { d } c ^ { b } } } \\{ { \qquad = D _ { \mu } ^ { a h } ( \delta _ { \scriptscriptstyle \mathrm { B } } c ^ { h } ) - ( \delta ^ { a h } \partial _ { \mu } - g f ^ { a h e } A _ { \mu } ^ { e } ) { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } g f ^ { b c h } c ^ { c } c ^ { b } } } \\{ { \qquad = D _ { \mu } ^ { a h } ( \delta _ { \scriptscriptstyle \mathrm { B } } c ^ { h } + { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } g f ^ { b c h } c ^ { b } c ^ { c } ) . } } \end{array} \tag{74.14}
	$$
</synced_block>
We see that this vanishes if the BRST variation of the ghost field is given by eq. (74.10).
<callout color="gray_bg">
	<synced_block url="https://app.notion.com/p/51a0dad3c8454b07a2087d974003aaf0#ab87949f1d7f40bdb3df26ed2f80b331">
		$$
		\delta _ { \mathrm { B } } c ^ { c } ( x ) = - { \textstyle \frac { 1 } { 2 } } g f ^ { a b c } c ^ { a } ( x ) c ^ { b } ( x ) . \tag{74.10}
		$$
	</synced_block>
</callout>
Now we introduce the antighost field $`\bar { c } ^ { a } ( x )`$ . We take its BRST transformation to be
<synced_block url="https://app.notion.com/p/51a0dad3c8454b07a2087d974003aaf0#30bcf2fee7de4843b969808bd36755aa">
	$$
	\delta _ { \mathrm { B } } \bar { c } ^ { a } ( x ) = B ^ { a } ( x ) , \tag{74.15}
	$$
</synced_block>
where $`B ^ { a } ( x )`$ is a commuting (as opposed to Grassmann) scalar field, the Lautrup–Nakanishi auxiliary field. Because $`B ^ { a } ( x )`$ is itself a BRST variation, we have
<synced_block url="https://app.notion.com/p/51a0dad3c8454b07a2087d974003aaf0#8fc691f70ad940a0a69c256ed85d26ee">
	$$
	\delta _ { \mathrm { B } } B ^ { a } ( x ) = 0 . \tag{74.16}
	$$
</synced_block>
Note that eq. (74.15) is in apparent contradiction with eq. (74.10). However, there is actually no need to identify $`\bar { c } ^ { a } ( x )`$ as the hermitian conjugate of $`c ^ { a } ( x )`$ . The role of these fields (in producing the functional determinant that must accompany the gauge-fixing delta functional) is fulfilled as long as $`c ^ { a } ( x )`$ and $`\bar { c } ^ { a } ( x )`$ are treated as independent when we integrate them; whether or not they are hermitian conjugates of each other is irrelevant. We identified them as hermitian conjugates in section 71 only for the sake of familiarity in deriving the associated Feynman rules. Now, however, we must abandon this notion. In fact, it will be most convenient to treat $`c ^ { a } ( x )`$ and $`\bar { c } ^ { a } ( x )`$ as two real Grassmann fields.
<callout color="gray_bg">
	<synced_block url="https://app.notion.com/p/51a0dad3c8454b07a2087d974003aaf0#593520fa353a4f9b975fe6c722233202">
		$$
		\delta _ { \mathrm { B } } \bar { c } ^ { a } ( x ) = B ^ { a } ( x ) , \tag{74.15}
		$$
	</synced_block>
	<synced_block url="https://app.notion.com/p/51a0dad3c8454b07a2087d974003aaf0#a8b39f41dd1b447a9011e9398121eee7">
		$$
		\delta _ { \mathrm { B } } c ^ { c } ( x ) = - { \textstyle \frac { 1 } { 2 } } g f ^ { a b c } c ^ { a } ( x ) c ^ { b } ( x ) . \tag{74.10}
		$$
	</synced_block>
</callout>
Now that we have introduced a collection of new fields— $`c ^ { a } ( x )`$ , $`\bar { c } ^ { a } ( x )`$ , and $`B ^ { a } ( x )`$ —what are we to do with them?
Consider adding to $`\mathcal { L } _ { \mathrm { Y M } }`$ a new term that is the BRST variation of some object $`\mathcal { O }`$ ,
<synced_block url="https://app.notion.com/p/51a0dad3c8454b07a2087d974003aaf0#d88c062c64094dc2885048c0dda4e1ff">
	$$
	\mathcal { L } = \mathcal { L } _ { \mathrm { Y M } } + \delta _ { \mathrm { B } } \mathcal { O } . \tag{74.17}
	$$
</synced_block>
Clearly $`\mathcal { L }`$ is BRST invariant, because $`\mathcal { L } _ { \mathrm { v M } }`$ is, and because $`\delta _ { \mathrm { B } } ( \delta _ { \mathrm { B } } \mathcal { O } ) = 0`$ . We will see that adding $`\delta _ { \mathrm { { B } } } \mathcal { O }`$ corresponds to fixing a gauge; which gauge we get depends on $`\mathcal { O }`$ .
We will choose
<synced_block url="https://app.notion.com/p/51a0dad3c8454b07a2087d974003aaf0#a3ae572a568f450faa47e1d67f3d823a">
	$$
	{ \mathcal O } ( x ) = \bar { c } ^ { a } ( x ) \Bigl [ { \textstyle \frac { 1 } { 2 } } \xi B ^ { a } ( x ) - { G } ^ { a } ( x ) \Bigr ] , \tag{74.18}
	$$
</synced_block>
where $`G ^ { a } ( x )`$ is a gauge-fixing function, and $`\xi`$ is a parameter. If we further choose
<synced_block url="https://app.notion.com/p/51a0dad3c8454b07a2087d974003aaf0#536adb77682149539a8755e80607de33">
	$$
	G ^ { a } ( x ) = \partial ^ { \mu } A _ { \mu } ^ { a } ( x ) , \tag{74.19}
	$$
</synced_block>
then we end up with $`R _ { \xi }`$ gauge.
Let us see how this works. We have
<synced_block url="https://app.notion.com/p/51a0dad3c8454b07a2087d974003aaf0#f37a25ec3cb34fe9946a2735126c2522">
	$$
	\delta _ { \mathrm { s } } \mathcal { O } = \left( \delta _ { \mathrm { s } } \bar { c } ^ { a } \right) \bigg [ { \textstyle \frac { 1 } { 2 } } \xi B ^ { a } - \partial ^ { \mu } A _ { \mu } ^ { a } \bigg ] - \bar { c } ^ { a } \bigg [ { \textstyle \frac { 1 } { 2 } } \xi \big ( \delta _ { \mathrm { s } } B ^ { a } \big ) - \partial ^ { \mu } \big ( \delta _ { \mathrm { s } } A _ { \mu } ^ { a } \big ) \bigg ] ~ . \tag{74.20}
	$$
</synced_block>
There is a minus sign in front of the second set of terms because $`\delta _ { \mathrm { { B } } }`$ acts as an anticommuting object, and so it generates a minus sign when it passes through another anticommuting object, in this case $`{ \bar { c } } ^ { a }`$ . Now using eqs. (74.3), (74.15), and (74.16), we get
<callout color="gray_bg">
	<synced_block url="https://app.notion.com/p/51a0dad3c8454b07a2087d974003aaf0#4b7aba81fff2422488c1e32ffb0fdd4a">
		$$
		\begin{array} { l } { { \delta _ { \mathrm { { s } } } A _ { \mu } ^ { a } ( x ) \equiv D _ { \mu } ^ { a b } c ^ { b } ( x ) } } \\{ { { } } } \\{ { { } = \partial _ { \mu } c ^ { a } ( x ) - g f ^ { a b c } A _ { \mu } ^ { c } ( x ) c ^ { b } ( x ) , } } \end{array} \tag{74.3}
		$$
	</synced_block>
	<synced_block url="https://app.notion.com/p/51a0dad3c8454b07a2087d974003aaf0#8e2b923e91624b3aad63b03d5efa0546">
		$$
		\delta _ { \mathrm { B } } \bar { c } ^ { a } ( x ) = B ^ { a } ( x ) , \tag{74.15}
		$$
	</synced_block>
	<synced_block url="https://app.notion.com/p/51a0dad3c8454b07a2087d974003aaf0#6ef0669fa9024955ae536b0651cb8d3c">
		$$
		\delta _ { \mathrm { B } } B ^ { a } ( x ) = 0 . \tag{74.16}
		$$
	</synced_block>
</callout>
<synced_block url="https://app.notion.com/p/51a0dad3c8454b07a2087d974003aaf0#d419d319054d45bf9513203492d66ebb">
	$$
	\delta _ { \scriptscriptstyle \mathrm { B } } { \mathcal O } = \textstyle { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } \xi B ^ { a } B ^ { a } - B ^ { a } \partial ^ { \mu } A _ { \mu } ^ { a } + \bar { c } ^ { a } \partial ^ { \mu } D _ { \mu } ^ { a b } c ^ { b } . \tag{74.21}
	$$
</synced_block>
We see that the last term is the ghost lagrangian $`{ \mathcal { L } } _ { \mathrm { g h } }`$ that we found in section 71. If we like, we can integrate the ordinary derivative by parts, so that it acts on the antighost field,
<synced_block url="https://app.notion.com/p/51a0dad3c8454b07a2087d974003aaf0#ac29e315fa274470b1ca0bbdaa2c9b09">
	$$
	\delta _ { \scriptscriptstyle \mathrm { B } } \mathcal { O } \to { \textstyle \frac { 1 } { 2 } } \xi B ^ { a } B ^ { a } - B ^ { a } \partial ^ { \mu } A _ { \mu } ^ { a } - \partial ^ { \mu } \bar { c } ^ { a } D _ { \mu } ^ { a b } c ^ { b } . \tag{74.22}
	$$
</synced_block>
Examining the first two terms in eq. (74.22), we see that no derivatives act on the auxiliary field $`B ^ { a } ( x )`$ . Furthermore, it appears only quadratically and linearly in $`\delta _ { \mathrm { { B } } } \mathcal { O }`$ . We can, therefore, perform the path integral over it; the result is equivalent to solving the classical equation of motion
<callout color="gray_bg">

Finally, we note that the vacuum $`| 0 \rangle`$ must be in the cohomology, because it is the unique state with zero energy and positive norm.
Thus we can conclude that we can build an initial state of widely separated particles that is in the cohomology only if we do not include any ghost or antighost particles, or photons with polarizations other than $`^ +`$ and $`-`$ . Since a state in the cohomology must evolve to another state in the cohomology, no ghosts, antighosts, or unphysically polarized photons can be produced in the scattering process.
Reference notes
A detailed treatment of BRST symmetry can be found in Weinberg II.
## Problems
### 74.1
The creation operator for a photon of positive helicity can be written as
<synced_block url="https://app.notion.com/p/51a0dad3c8454b07a2087d974003aaf0#100fbc3be1ed448f997cf78cd5757594">
	$$
	a _ { + } ^ { \dagger } ( { \bf k } ) = - i \varepsilon _ { + } ^ { \mu * } ( { \bf k } ) \int d ^ { 3 } x e ^ { + i k x } \overleftrightarrow { \partial _ { 0 } } A _ { \mu } ( x ) . \tag{74.42}
	$$
</synced_block>
Consider the state $`a _ { + } ^ { \dag } ( { \bf k } ) | \psi \rangle`$ , where $`| \psi \rangle`$ is in the BRST cohomology. Define a gauge-transformed polarization vector
<synced_block url="https://app.notion.com/p/51a0dad3c8454b07a2087d974003aaf0#cb7e0cf8527f4359af7b8a8725a664e6">
	$$
	\tilde { \varepsilon } _ { + } ^ { \mu } ( { \bf k } ) = \varepsilon _ { + } ^ { \mu } ( { \bf k } ) + c k ^ { \mu } , \tag{74.43}
	$$
</synced_block>
where $`c`$ is a constant, and a corresponding creation operator $`\tilde { a } _ { + } ^ { \dagger } ( \mathbf { k } )`$ . Show that
<synced_block url="https://app.notion.com/p/51a0dad3c8454b07a2087d974003aaf0#a3dacb05d12f46e19c2bf8ed52f219ab">
	$$
	\tilde { a } _ { + } ^ { \dagger } ( { \bf k } ) | \psi \rangle = a _ { + } ^ { \dagger } ( { \bf k } ) | \psi \rangle + Q _ { \mathrm { { B } } } | \chi \rangle , \tag{74.44}
	$$
</synced_block>
which implies that $`\tilde { a } _ { + } ^ { \dagger } ( { \bf k } ) | \psi \rangle`$ and $`a _ { + } ^ { \dagger } ( { \bf k } ) | \psi \rangle`$ represent the same element of the cohomology, and hence are physically equivalent. Find the state $`| \chi \rangle`$ .
